name: libPhenom
workload: tests/bench/iopipes.t event-dispatch benchmark: many pipe/socket descriptors made readable in a loop, counting events fired per second on a single core (-c 1) over about 1 second, with libphenom's nbio scheduler versus libevent (-e flag); the commit message does not state the descriptor count (the tool defaults to 100).
claimed_speedup: Commit message 'Streamline nbio scheduling a bit' (Jun 2013): 'we're a bit faster because we're doing overall less book keeping per event'. Linux: libphenom 366,624 events/s vs libevent 264,129 events/s (about 1.39x, derived from page data). OSX: libphenom 505,155 events/s vs libevent 471,385 events/s (about 1.07x, derived from page data). The OSX and Linux numbers come from different machines.
hardware: Not stated; the commit says the OSX and Linux numbers came from two different machines. Single core only.
stars_or_usage: 1.7k stars; repository archived 2019-03-09 (README points to folly as the maintained alternative)
tradeoffs: C99 eventing framework (epoll, kqueue, port_create) with its own job scheduler, buffers, hash tables and JSON variants; depends on Concurrency Kit and OpenSSL; any IO thread can service any descriptor (no thread affinity), so more threads add events/s but with a falling per-core rate on the iopipes workload (commit message).
caveats: First-party, single 1-second runs from one commit message in June 2013; hardware, compiler, flags and libevent version are all unstated, and OSX and Linux numbers came from different machines. The commit itself calls the result a 'gut check'. Benchmark code (tests/bench/iopipes.c, run-pipes.php, phenom.R) is public, but no charts or later numbers are checked in, and the multi-descriptor scaling charts the scripts generate were not found. The project is archived and unmaintained since 2019, and libevent has moved on since 2013. The README itself says only 'high performance and high scalability' with no numbers.

name: libpopcnt
baseline: scalar POPCNT instruction loop (the __builtin_popcountll / std::popcount style baseline) and the library's own earlier Harley-Seal AVX2 path
workload: Counting 1 bits in a byte array of 96 bytes to 1 KB using a plain AVX2 popcnt256 loop instead of scalar POPCNT or Harley-Seal (libpopcnt 4.2 ChangeLog entry); the repo's benchmark program otherwise times popcnt() over fixed array sizes (23, 101, 1001, 10001, 16384 bytes in CI).
claimed_speedup: ChangeLog 4.2: 'Up to 3x faster popcount for medium arrays (96 bytes to 1 KB) using a simple AVX2 popcnt256 loop instead of scalar POPCNT or Harley-Seal.' Also 'Up to 6x faster on old x86 CPUs without POPCNT' (baseline not named) and README example of 133.5 GB/s for a 16 KB array with the AVX512 algorithm (no baseline given).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the ChangeLog claims; README says build with -O3 or -O2 and no -mavx2 needed (runtime CPUID dispatch).
hardware: ChangeLog claims: not stated. README example run: AMD EPYC 9R14 (2023), AVX512 algorithm, 16 KB array.
stars_or_usage: 370 stars; Rust port exists as the simd-popcnt crate
tradeoffs: Header-only; runtime CPUID dispatch (POPCNT, AVX2, AVX512 VPOPCNTDQ, ARM NEON, SVE, PPC64 POPCNTD, portable fallback); no special compiler flags needed; thread-safe. Only counts bits in a byte array (no bitset container).
caveats: Weak evidence for an outside baseline: the library's benchmark program and CI only compare the current code against its own previous release (fail if more than 2% slower), and the only 'faster than' numbers are ChangeLog lines whose hardware, compiler and baseline code are not given; the 3x figure compares libpopcnt's new medium-array path with its own older scalar POPCNT or Harley-Seal path, not with an external library. The AVX2 Harley-Seal algorithm comes from the Mula, Kurz and Lemire paper 'Faster Population Counts using AVX2 Instructions' and the sse-popcount repository (peer-reviewed numbers for the algorithm, not opened here because arXiv is blocked and sse-popcount's README holds no tables), so the paper's numbers are not attributed to libpopcnt. The suggested category (filesystems-and-io) was wrong; this is a bit-count primitive.

name: mtrebi/memory-allocators (free list allocator; linear, stack and pool allocators)
baseline: malloc/free (libc; the benchmark's CAllocator wraps malloc and free)
workload: Time to Init() the allocator and then perform N allocations (and frees) of fixed or randomly chosen sizes (32 to 4096 bytes, alignment 8) single-threaded, charted against number of operations up to about 1 million for block size 4096; custom linear, stack, pool and free-list allocators versus malloc.
claimed_speedup: README 'Time complexity': 'Malloc is without doubt the worst allocator'; 'Free list allocator is a much better choice than malloc as a general purpose allocator ... It's about three times better than malloc'; linear, stack and pool allocators are faster still but restricted (pool: one fixed size; stack: LIFO frees; linear: no single frees). Exact figures only appear in two chart images (read off the no-Init chart at about 1M operations, block 4096: malloc roughly 1500 ms, free list roughly 360 ms, pool roughly 80 ms, stack and linear roughly 20 ms; approximate, not text on the page).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. CMakeLists.txt sets only cxx_std_11 and the README build command passes no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so a default build has no optimization flags unless the user adds them.
tradeoffs: Educational implementations: linear (no per-item free), stack (LIFO), pool (single block size) and a first-fit linked-list free-list allocator with minimum-size and alignment constraints; no thread safety, no size classes, no red-black-tree free list (listed as future work).
caveats: First-party, tier C: no hardware, compiler, flags or libc version stated, and the repo's default build has no optimization flags. Benchmark code is public (src/Benchmark.cpp, src/main.cpp) but Benchmark.h currently defines OPERATIONS as 10 (the `#if 0` branch that would use the operation count is disabled and the address arrays are sized OPERATIONS), so the shipped binary runs only 10 operations per round and cannot reproduce the README's roughly 1M-operation charts without editing. The timed region includes Init() (one large malloc plus setup), which the README itself says distorts the curves. The charts predate later commits that rewrote the pool allocator initialization (2026-04) and stack allocator. The three-times claim is for the free list only; the faster allocators drop general-purpose semantics. Baseline is plain libc malloc, not jemalloc, tcmalloc or mimalloc.

name: NVthreads
baseline: Atlas (HP persistent-memory failure-atomic-section library) and Mnemosyne (word-level STM persistent memory); plain pthreads is faster than NVthreads
workload: Making multi-threaded programs durable on emulated NVM (tmpfs with 1000 ns delay per 4 KB page write): 14 Phoenix and PARSEC benchmarks with 12 threads against Atlas, a 4 MB-per-4-threads page-modification microbenchmark against Atlas and Mnemosyne, and PageRank (Slashdot graph and LiveJournal) against both.
claimed_speedup: EuroSys 2017 paper: 'NVthreads is 2x-10x faster than Mnemosyne and more than 2x faster than Atlas'; 'in 10 out of the 12 workloads on which Atlas ran, NVthreads is from 7% to 100x faster depending upon the workload' (NVthreads about 7% and 50% slower than Atlas on streamcluster and reverse index); microbenchmark 'NVthreads is 3x-30x faster than these systems'; PageRank on the Slashdot graph at 12 cores: 170 ms per iteration vs 500 ms Atlas (about 2.9x, derived from page data) and 5 s Mnemosyne (about 29x, derived from page data); LiveJournal: 5 s vs 29 s Atlas, 'almost 6x faster'. Against plain pthreads it is slower: 9 of 14 apps under 28% overhead, but canneal, dedup, ferret and reverse index over 4x.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper; the library's src/Makefile builds with -O3 -DNDEBUG -msse2 -fPIC.
hardware: Two Intel Xeon X5650 (12 cores at 2.67 GHz), 198 GB RAM, 600 GB SSD, Ubuntu 14.04 (Linux 3.16.7); NVM emulated with a modified tmpfs on DRAM adding 1000 ns per 4 KB page write
tradeoffs: Drop-in pthreads replacement that adds persistence: Dthreads-style multi-process execution with copy-on-write page buffering, page-granularity redo logs and recovery; overhead versus plain pthreads is 20 to 28% on easy workloads and over 4x on others; needs an NVM filesystem; research prototype ('use at your own risk'); log space 165 MB to 300 MB versus 550 MB-3.2 GB for Mnemosyne in the microbenchmark.
caveats: The baselines are other persistence systems, not std::thread or pthreads, so the guessed baseline (std::thread) does not apply and NVthreads is slower than unmodified pthreads. NVM is emulated; Atlas could not run canneal and dedup, Mnemosyne ran only the microbenchmark and a small PageRank graph (it crashes above 4 MB of durable data), and the Mnemosyne 2 s fork overhead was excluded. Compiler flags for the benchmark applications are not stated in the paper. License file is GPL-2.0 (COPYING) while the awesome-cpp listing says LGPL-2.1, and the tree vendors Atlas, Mnemosyne and Dthreads code under their own licenses. Category thread-pools-work-stealing is the closest fit among wave-11 categories; the project is really persistent-memory threading.

name: NCCL
workload: Allreduce latency by message size between two servers with 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs each, over 100 Gbps InfiniBand RDMA and over TCP/IP sockets, NCCL 2.3.7 versus Gloo commit 1d9e62a, 5000 iterations (user-posted GitHub issue).
claimed_speedup: gloo issue #158 (Dec 2018, user report): IB RDMA: 256 KB allreduce 0.13 ms (NCCL) vs 20.161 ms (Gloo); 128 KB 0.09 ms vs 1.073 ms; 64 KB 0.13 ms vs 0.155 ms. TCP/IP: 512 KB 7.12 ms vs 20.544 ms; 1 MB 11.91 ms vs 39.855 ms; 2 MB 20.9 ms vs 78.237 ms. At 1 KB Gloo was faster (0.039 ms vs 0.16 ms for NCCL on IB RDMA).
hardware: Two Ubuntu servers with 8 V100 GPUs each; 100 Gbps IB RDMA (test 1) or TCP/IP sockets (test 2); CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: GPU-only collectives (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce, broadcast, reduce-scatter, send/recv) over PCIe, NVLink, NVSwitch, InfiniBand verbs and TCP sockets; NVIDIA GPUs and CUDA required; mostly Apache-2.0 with BSD parts (LICENSE.txt), although the README still carries an 'all rights reserved' 2015-2020 notice.
caveats: Weak evidence for such a notable project: the only reachable numbers are one user's report filed against Gloo (reporter complained Gloo is slow for large allreduce); no maintainer reply was visible, the NCCL-side command and buffer placement are not shown, and Gloo's benchmark tool may have used CPU buffers and the ring algorithm rather than its GPU or bcube paths. Versions are from 2018 (NCCL 2.3.7). NCCL lost at 1 KB. The repository README and nccl-tests README carry no baseline numbers; published NCCL-versus-MPI studies (for example an MVAPICH2-GDR paper reporting up to 14x lower small-message broadcast latency than NCCL, and an AlexNet/ResNet allreduce paper that reports NCCL throughput gains over OpenMPI) exist on arXiv but arXiv and the NVIDIA developer blog are blocked here, so none could be opened or quoted. Category and domain are a best fit (GPU collective communication has no dedicated category); the guessed thread-pools category was wrong.
